items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: And so when I saw Ray after that I said “Ray, were you the first one to do that?” He said “no, you were the first one.”

ctx.x: How did, I meant to ask this earlier on, but how did the double bass drum set come to fruition? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

Well Eddie Shaughnessy came to me once and he said “hey, did you really start the two bass drums? I thought you did, but did Ray McKinley do it first?” I said well I don’t know because when I was a youngster in 1938 I drew the plans for the double bass drum kit. And around 1940, I saw in Down Beat where Ray McKinley was teamed with Will Bradley. They had a band together. They did a lot of boogie woogie things. And there was a picture of him with just two bass drums, see? And so when I saw Ray after that I said…
It must have helped to be a tap dancer I would think.

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When I finally saw him, he said, “No. You were the first one, Lou.”

ctx.x: A lot of people point to Ray McKinley using double bass drums. It sounds like you preceded him at least as far as the idea.

I thought he was the first one, but later on he told me, “No. It was you. You were the first one.” He came up – he was with Will Bradley’s band. Double Drum Boogie came up with him. He had two bass drums, and he played them with mallets. I thought – I kept giving people the idea that Ray was the first one. When I finally saw him, he said, “No. You were the first one, Lou.” I said, “You’re older than I am, so I figured [it was] from you.”
Did he actually have two pedals on it, or was he just using the bass drums and playing them with his hands.
